title: How a Church Should Communicate
subtitle: Why most church communication problems are really clarity problems, how to choose the right channels, and why a healthy church over-communicates the few things that matter and stops drowning its people in noise.

sections.title: It Was Never a Communication Problem
sections.body:
When a church says it has a communication problem, it is almost always saying something else and does not know it. It is saying it has a clarity problem, and clarity is upstream of communication.

You cannot communicate what you have not decided. The announcement is muddy because the plan is muddy. The congregation is confused about the direction because the leadership is confused about the direction and has been hiding that confusion behind better graphics and more emails. No newsletter solves this. No app solves this. You can broadcast fog in high definition and it is still fog.

I spent a year trying to fix our communication. New systems, new platforms, a volunteer to run it all. None of it worked, and it took me embarrassingly long to understand why. We were not failing to tell people things. We were failing to know our own mind, and the people felt the wobble underneath every confident announcement.

Let your yes be yes and your no be no, Jesus said. The first act of good communication is not saying it well. It is having something true and settled to say. Decide first. Then speak.

sections.title: Say One Thing, Clearly
sections.body:
The enemy of being heard is not silence. It is volume. Most churches do not under-inform their people. They bury them, and a buried message is as good as an unsent one.

A bulletin with forty announcements communicates nothing, because it asks the hearer to do the prioritizing the leader refused to do. If everything is bolded, nothing is. The congregation learns, correctly, that none of it is essential, because a leader who knew what was essential would have said less and said it louder.

Good communication requires the courage to choose. What are the two or three things this church actually needs to know and do this season. Say those relentlessly. Let the rest live somewhere quieter, available to those who go looking, absent from the center where it would only dilute the few things that matter.

If the trumpet does not sound a clear call, Paul asked, who will get ready for battle. He was talking about tongues, but the principle holds for every announcement slide and every all-church email. An unclear signal is not partial communication. It is no communication, with extra steps.

sections.title: The Message Decides the Channel
sections.body:
Not every message belongs everywhere, and the leader who treats all channels as interchangeable trains his people to ignore all of them equally.

The weight of the message should set the channel. A schedule change is an email. A vision shift is a sermon and a series of conversations and a letter the pastor actually signed. A correction to a rumor is spoken in person to the people who heard the rumor, not posted publicly where it announces a problem to people who never knew there was one. Match the medium to the weight, or you will deliver heavy things in light containers and watch them shatter.

The most important things in a church do not travel well through screens. The vision, the rebuke, the comfort, the call. These need a face, a voice, a body in the room. Jesus had the whole of Scripture available to teach from, and he still chose mostly to teach by being present, eating with people, walking the road, letting his life carry the message his words could only point at.

Use the tools. The app and the email and the text are good servants. They are terrible substitutes for a pastor who shows up and says the hard thing himself.

sections.title: Say It Until You Are Sick of It
sections.body:
Here is the part that offends the leader's ego. By the time you are exhausted with saying something, your congregation is hearing it for roughly the first time.

You live inside the vision. You think about it daily, refine it, dream about it. They hear it for ninety seconds on a Sunday they happened to attend, between a sick child and a work deadline and the forty other voices competing for their week. The gap between your saturation and their attention is enormous, and the leader who quits repeating because he is bored has confused his own fatigue for their comprehension.

The healthy church over-communicates the essential few things to the point of redundancy. It says the mission again. It tells the story again. It explains the why behind the what again, because people forget the why and keep only the what, and a what without a why dies the moment it becomes inconvenient.

Moses told Israel to bind the commands on their hands, set them as frontlets between their eyes, write them on their doorposts, teach them to their children, speak of them sitting and walking and lying down and rising up. That is not a man worried about saying it too often. That is a leader who understood that the things that matter most are precisely the things people forget fastest.

sections.title: Where You Are Silent, Fear Speaks
sections.body:
There is one more thing, and it is the one that costs churches the most. In the absence of communication from leadership, communication does not stop. It simply changes authors.

When you do not explain the decision, people explain it for you, and their explanation is almost always worse than the truth. When you go quiet during the crisis, the silence does not read as calm. It reads as hiding, and the parking lot fills with theories you would have prevented with three honest sentences. Where the shepherd will not speak, fear and rumor speak in his place, and they are fluent and tireless and never off the clock.

This is why courage is the hidden skill underneath all church communication. Not eloquence. Courage. The willingness to say the hard thing before it leaks, to name the problem before the rumor names it for you, to stand in front of your people in the uncertain moment and tell them what you know and admit what you do not.

A church does not need a perfect communicator at the front. It needs an honest one who will not leave a vacuum for fear to fill. Speak. Speak clearly, speak the weighty things in person, speak the essential things until you are weary of them, and never let your silence become the loudest voice in the room.
